The editorial framing (trap/hinge/gravity/synthesis/claim/say/do/subtract) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. [Authored 2026-10-06, Opus, Phase 4b brief, born v2: the build carries one track ('single'). The store has NO Catena Aurea Fathers on Mark (Calvin, Matthew Henry, Barnes and JFB are index-only rows; Barth's two pointers sit on Mark 13:9-13, outside the pericope), so the Gospel doors rest on the Glossa ordinaria (Migne) 13:25, 13:31, 13:32, 13:34 and 13:36, Wesley's Notes 13:32 and 13:34, and the Catena intertext notes on Mark 13 (Daniel 12:7-9, Isaiah 21:6-8, Isaiah 40:8). Catena Aurea on the Matthew 24 parallel was deliberately not borrowed: it is not attested on this passage. Isaiah 64 doors from Glossa 64:1, 64:4, 64:8, Wesley 64:1, 64:4, 64:6, 64:8, and Catena intertext notes (taken up at Mark 1:9-11, 1 Cor 2:6-9, 2 Cor 4:7); the Glossa's 64:6 gloss was left aside. Psalm 80 rows (Glossa 80:1, 80:19; Wesley 80:3) inform gravity/synthesis only. Not used on the Gospel: the Glossa's fig-tree-as-Synagogue reading (13:28) and Hilary's Trinitarian gloss on 13:32.]
trap: The text gets turned into a countdown: signs read off the news, dates guessed, and a sermon that frightens people into alertness. Or, in the first week of December, it is softened into a cozy season of waiting for Christmas, and "keep awake" becomes a vague call to be more mindful. The first makes watching anxious and the second makes it optional.
hinge: Jesus says the sky will fall and his words will not, and then says that even the Son does not know the day or the hour. The coming is certain and the timing is withheld, and he builds the command to keep awake on exactly that gap. A preacher cannot close the gap from either side, by predicting the hour or by assuming it will not come.

doors.claim: God keeps the day hidden on purpose and for our good. A people who cannot know when the Lord will come are free to live every day as though he might come tomorrow.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Neither the Son. Therefore hidden, because it is not expedient for us to know. In which he shows that he knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, being always uncertain of the coming of the judge, they may live daily as though they were to be judged on the morrow. The Son therefore knows for himself, but not for us, that we may always be watchful.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Of that day — The day of judgment is often in the Scriptures emphatically called that day. Neither the Son - Not as man: as man he was no more omniscient than omnipresent. But as God he knows all the circumstances of it.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Daniel is told 'the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end' — the timing of the consummation is withheld even from the seer. Mark's 'no one knows the day or hour' continues this Danielic tradition. (Echo of Daniel 12:7–9)

doors.say: You don't know when he is coming, and that isn't a gap in your information. It is a gift: it means today counts.
doors.do: Ask them to name one thing they keep putting off until "someday", such as a reconciliation, a confession, or a gift, and to do it this week as if the Lord were coming on the morrow.

doors.landing: Each at the post he gave
doors.claim: The absent master has not left his house empty. He has given each servant authority and a task, and stationed a doorkeeper. To watch is to stay awake at the work he gave you, keeping the door of your own heart.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The Son of man is as a man taking a far journey — Being about to leave this world and go to the Father, he appoints the services that are to be performed by all his servants, in their several stations. This seems chiefly to respect ministers at the day of judgment: but it may be applied to all men, and to the time of death.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And what I say to you. Not only the rulers of the Church, but all of us are bidden to watch, keeping the doors of our hearts; lest the evil suggestion of the ancient enemy steal in, lest the Lord find us sleeping.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Watch ye therefore. He who sleeps sees not bodies, but phantasms, and when he awakes he has nothing of those things which he had seen. Such are they whom the love of the world snatches away in life, and forsakes after life.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Go, set a watchman... Upon a watchtower I stand continually by day, and at my post whole nights' provides the prophetic figure of the sentinel keeping watch through the night-watches. Mark's doorkeeper told to 'keep watch' and the listing of evening/midnight/cockcrow/morning watches draw on this watchman tradition. (Allusion of Isaiah 21:6–8)

doors.say: Watching doesn't mean staring at the sky. It means being found awake at the work he left in your hands, with the door of your heart kept.
doors.do: Have them name their station (home, job, pew, neighbourhood) and the one task the Master left them there, and do it this week as a servant who expects him home.

doors.landing: The heavens shake; his words stand
doors.claim: Everything that looks permanent will give way: sun, moon, stars, the powers of heaven. The words of the one who first came down in humility will not, and he comes again on the clouds.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: What wonder is it that men should tremble, when at the sight of the judgment the angelic powers tremble? They shall be moved. To the wrath of vengeance, when they shall be sent by the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power, who before came down in humility like rain upon a fleece.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Heaven and earth shall pass away. So therefore heaven and earth pass away according to their image, they remain for ever according to their essence.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever' is the closest source for the permanence of God's word over against transient creation. Mark transfers the abiding-word of Isaiah 40 to 'my words,' an implicit christological claim. (Allusion of Isaiah 40:8)

doors.say: The lights you steer by may go out. The one who came down as quietly as rain on a fleece has given you a word that will outlast the sky.
doors.do: Invite them to name one 'star' they have been steering by (a market, an institution, a leader) and to set one word of Christ beside it to steer by this Advent.

doors.claim: The prayer does not ask God to be nearer in feeling. It asks him to break through, the way someone desperate to help a friend breaks down the door, and the gospel answers it at the Jordan.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Rent — A metaphor taken from men, that when they would resolutely help one in distress, break and fling open doors and whatever may hinder. Flow down - That all impediments might be removed out of the way: possibly an allusion to God's coming down upon Mount Sinai, in those terrible flames of fire.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: O that thou wouldst rend. In his own person ... likewise David: He bowed the heavens, and came down.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Mark's distinctive 'the heavens being torn' (schizomenous) recalls Isaiah 64:1 LXX, 'O that you would rend the heavens and come down.' Coherence is high: God rends the heavens to descend in the Spirit upon Jesus. (taken up at Mark 1:9–11)

doors.say: Isaiah wanted God to tear the sky open and come down. Advent is the church learning to pray that again, and remembering that he did.
doors.do: Have them pray Isaiah 64:1 daily this week over one situation where they need God to break through, not merely to comfort.

doors.claim: The confession goes all the way down, so that even our righteousness is a soiled rag and we fade like leaves. Then the prayer turns on one word, 'Father': look on your work, not our merits.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: And all - The very best of us all are no better than the uncleanest things. Taken - Carried away to Babylon, as leaves hurried away by a boisterous wind.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And now, O Lord. As if he should say: If we consider our own merits, we must despair; if thy clemency, who scourgest every son whom thou receivest, we dare to pour out prayers, for thou art our father. The works of thy hands. As if he should say: Look upon thy work, not upon our merits.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Our father — Notwithstanding all this thou art our father both by creation, and by adoption, therefore pity us thy children.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'We are the clay, you our potter' establishes the creature-as-vessel theme that Paul presses to magnify God's power over human weakness. (taken up at 2 Corinthians 4:7)

doors.say: When there is nothing left to plead, Isaiah pleads who God is: "Yet you are our Father. We are the clay." Don't look at what we made of ourselves. Look at what your hands made.
doors.do: Lead them in a confession that names honestly what has withered, and then hands it to God with the words of verse 8.

doors.claim: God acts for those who wait for him, and what he prepares is more than the eye has seen or the heart has imagined. Waiting is not empty time; something is being made ready.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Besides thee — This is to be applied to all the wonderful works, that God at all times wrought for his people: and thus they are a plea with God, that they might well expect such things from him now, that had done such wonderful things for their fathers. Waiteth - This may be taken with reference both to the state of grace and glory, those incomprehensible things that are exhibited through Christ in the mysteries of the gospel.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: From the beginning of the world. Hence Paul, writing to the Corinthians, takes his testimony, not word for word, but expressing the sense. What the Apostle sets down, it hath not ascended into the heart of man, because it is greater, and the heart ought to be directed thither. For he prepared his very self, the knowledge of himself.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The explicit citation formula 'as it is written' introduces v.9, 'what no eye has seen, nor ear heard...what God has prepared for those who love him,' which most closely matches Isaiah 64:4 (LXX: God acts for those who wait/love him). (taken up at 1 Corinthians 2:6–9)

doors.say: What God is preparing for those who wait is not something we could have imagined. In the end, Isaiah's commentators said, it is God himself.
doors.do: Ask them to recall one 'wonderful work' God has done for them or their parents, and to make it this week's plea: you did this then, so we expect you now.

single.gravity: The year opens with a cry and a command. Isaiah begs God to tear the heavens open and come down, confessing that even our righteousness is a soiled rag and we fade like leaves, and still says "you are our Father; we are the clay" (Isaiah 64). The Psalm asks the Shepherd of Israel three times to restore us and let his face shine. Paul tells the Corinthians they lack nothing as they wait for the revealing of the Lord, who will keep them blameless to the end. Jesus says the heavens will shake, no one knows the hour, and "keep awake." The nerve: we ask God to come, and he tells us to be awake when he does.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah prays for the heavens to be torn open and pleads the Father's hand on his clay (Isaiah 64). The Psalm repeats "restore us, let your face shine, and we shall be saved" (Psalm 80). Paul tells a gifted, waiting church that God is faithful and will strengthen them to the end (1 Corinthians 1). Jesus answers the cry for God to come: the Son of Man will come on the clouds at an hour no one knows, so stay awake at your post (Mark 13). The prayer for God's coming and the command to watch are two halves of one Advent.
synthesis.claim: Pray for him to come, and be awake when he does, at the work he left you, trusting the faithful God who formed you.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that has grown used to God's absence, half-asleep at its work and quietly assuming nothing will break in, the move is to teach them Isaiah's bolder prayer (tear the heavens) and then hand them Jesus' quieter command: go back to your post and keep the door.

subtract: These three are doors, not points. Each is a different landing: the hidden hour as a gift, faithfulness at one's appointed post, and confidence when the heavens shake. Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and Catena intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus. Attested, not authored. (No Catena Aurea Fathers are on file for Mark.)
